catalog_quote: [Al-Tajir 1982, 'Stress in B', ebook PT72-73] Stress in this dialect, as in other dialects of Arabic, is determined by the syllabic components of a given form. In disyllabic forms, stress falls on: the initial syllable in the structure: CV-CV as in: šára (he bought); CV-CVC as in: ráṭil (one pound (weight)); CVV-CVC as in: máazaḥ (he joked); CVC-CVC as in: fállaʿ (he threw stones); the final syllable in the structure: CV-CVCC as in: labást (I dressed); CV-CVVC as in: nasíib (relative); CVC-CVVC as in: masdúud (blocked). In trisyllabic forms stress falls on: the initial syllable in the structure: CV-CV-CV as in: ḥáṭaba (wood); CV-CV-CVC as in: šárabat (she drank); the pre-final syllable in the structure: CV-CVV-CV as in: jamáara (people of Bani Jamrah); the final syllable in the structure: CV-CVV-CVVC as in: samaamíič (fisher folk); CV-CV-CVVC as in: gasamóoh (it was divided). In quadrisyllabic forms stress falls on the second syllable as in: CVC-CV-CV-CVC ʔindáʿamat (it was hit), ʔixtárabat (it broke down). [Holes 2016: 76, sec. 2.5 Stress, snippet text:] In all Bahraini dialects, stress falls on the last syllable of a word of two or more syllables if that syllable is long (CVC, CvCC), e.g. drubố-h, kitábt, ğālbút, duwālíb; otherwise, the penultimate syllable is stressed e.g. gálat, mgábil, yithawaš, mistášfa. ... In such forms the B ... antepenultimate: kátabat, wáraga. Stress is non-distinctive.

new_statements.quote: 2.5 Stress. In all Bahraini dialects, stress falls on the last syllable of a word of two or more syllables if that syllable is long (CV̄C, CvCC), e.g. drubṓ-h, kitábt, ǧālbū́t, duwālī́b; otherwise, the penultimate syllable is stressed e.g. gálat, mgábil, yitḥáwaš, mistášfa. [...] It should be noted that these stress rules apply after the vowel deletion rule that disallows sequences of more than two Cv short vowels (see 2.3.2). In the B dialects, but not in the A dialects, syllable structure rules allow sequences of short vowels (Cv-Cv-Cv) provided v1 is /a/, e.g. katabat 'she wrote' waraga 'leaf', (but A dialects ktibat, wriga). In such forms the B [...] antepenultimate: kátabat, wáraga. Stress is non-distinctive.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress the final syllable if it is heavy-long (Cv̄C or CvCC); otherwise stress the penult; in Baḥārna (B) forms with three light open syllables beginning Ca- (katabat, waraga), which survive only in B because B does not delete the first short vowel, stress is antepenultimate (kátabat, wáraga). Stress applies after short-vowel syncope and is not contrastive. Al-Tajir 1982 ('Stress in B') gives the same pattern structure by structure: CV-CV(C), CVV-CVC, CVC-CVC initial; CV-CVCC/CV(C)-CVVC final; CV-CV-CV(C) initial; CV-CVV-CV penult..-CVVC final; CVC-CV-CV-CVC second syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in the passages read.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb + prepositional clitic phrases are stressed as single words (gālat li -> gālát-li); final vowels of weak verbs and final diphthongs lengthen and attract stress under suffixation (yxálli / yxallī́-ni, báġa / baġā́-h, p. 79); some BU (urban Baḥārna, Ras Rummān) speakers extend this to strong verbs (dibḥā́-h). A (ʿArab) vs B (Baḥārna) differ only where B keeps Ca-Cv-Cv sequences (B kátabat vs A ktíbat).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for 'all Bahraini dialects' (A = ʿArab/Sunni and B = Baḥārna/Shiʿi), with the B-specific antepenult case singled out; phonological word includes verb + enclitic preposition. Examples are citation forms from Holes's 1970s fieldwork corpus.
new_statements.identity_note: Holes 2016 states the rule for 'all Bahraini dialects' and labels the two communal groups A (ʿArab, Sunni = Gulf Arabic, gulf1241) and B (Baḥārna, Shiʿi = baha1259); the antepenultimate-stress case (kátabat, wáraga) is explicitly a B-dialect (Baḥārna) property. Al-Tajir 1982 describes the Baḥārnah dialect ('B') specifically, contrasting it with the ʿAnazi/ʿArab ('A') dialect. Both therefore match baha1259 directly.
